newsitem.title: FRANCE: Paris should back Rome, Madrid on EMU - UDF party.
newsitem.headline: Paris should back Rome, Madrid on EMU - UDF party.

text.p: France should launch a trilateral initiative to back Spain and Italy's participation in European monetary union to ensure the euro zone is not simply a hunting ground for the countries of northern Europe, French UDF party leader Francois Leotard said.

"European monetary union can only be properly balanced if it is geographically and culturally balanced," said Leotard, whose political group is junior partner in the centre-right coalition of Prime Minister Alain Juppe.

"The Franco-German couple must not smother the voice of the Latin countries," Leotard, whose political base is in the south of France, said in an advance copy of an article which the UDF said would appear in Thursday's La Tribune newspaper.
"I believe a French initiative on this would be welcome," said Leotard.

"Why not take advantage of the lira's recent reentry into the European exchange rate mechanism to do so? It would be a question of reaffirming, in a trilateral context, France's support for the reforms which these countries have embarked on to meet the terms of the Maastricht EMU treaty."
"The three countries can, if they work in tandem, give our continent the scale, strength and flourish it needs," he said.
"Succeeding with all our partners, especially the Latin currencies, in the creation of the euro should become a major national objective," Leotard said.

Leotard, who took over as head of the UDF earlier this year from former president Valery Giscard d'Estaing, also weighed into a debate Giscard d'Estaing recently triggered in France about the possibility of depreciating the franc versus the mark.

"Devaluing the franc, or even more, turning back on the commitment to EMU, would not give us any further margin for manoeuvre, neither on interest rates nor on foreign trade, nor in the medium term on employment," he said.
"There is no added economic growth to be hope for from lax montary policy," he added.
Giscard d'Estaing recently raised the idea of depreciating the franc in remarks which were seized on by "eurosceptic" politicians to call for a switch in economic policy.
